structure.title: 4. Optimal Assignment Policy and Welfare Gains
5. Using the LATE Framework to Uncover the Mechanism

observations.statement: The estimand is a planner's social welfare functional over assignment policies, formally defined as an expectation over potential welfare contributions under a partition of the covariate space into three arms.

The paper names its data-generating design a doubly randomized preference trial, linking it to a hybrid sampling tradition in medical statistics that combines randomization with patient treatment choice.

An explicit exclusion-type assumption, that potential welfare outcomes do not depend on who chooses the treatment, is introduced and flagged as needed only for the mechanism analysis, not the main welfare results.
Individuals in the self-selection arm are partitioned into takers and non-takers by their observed take-up decision, and the LATE estimands are defined conditional on this latent partition.
A monotonicity condition needed for LATE identification is argued to hold automatically by construction of the three arms, since compliance is fixed by design for the compulsory arms.
The field experiment was fielded in summer 2020 in two Japanese regions in collaboration with a government ministry, following an invitation and pre-registration step for prospective participants.

The analysis sample is narrowed from pre-registered participants by dropping non-residential customers, mid-experiment contract cancellations, and households with incomplete high-frequency usage records.
The unit of observation is the household, randomly assigned to one of three arms in an unequal predetermined ratio favoring the compulsory arms because their data were intended for other studies.
The end-of-article replication statement notes that some underlying data are restricted and only partially releasable, with the journal separately granted temporary access to verify reproducibility.
Group sizes for each of the three randomized arms are reported in the running text and repeated in the note beneath the summary-statistics table.

The outcome used for policy assignment is a constructed household welfare contribution combining a price-cost wedge applied to the consumption change, a capacity-market benefit term, and a per-participant implementation cost, rather than raw usage.
Observed treatment take-up is defined separately from the randomly assigned arm, since only households assigned to the self-selection arm face a real choice about participation.
The randomly assigned arm indicator itself, rather than a separately constructed excluded variable, serves as the instrument for take-up in the LATE-style estimation.

Candidate covariates for the policy tree are narrowed to those flagged as important by both a lasso importance ranking and a causal-forest splitting-frequency ranking, keeping only variables selected by both methods.
Welfare-comparison tables place standard errors in parentheses directly beneath each point estimate rather than describing the standard-error method in a separate notes line.

Results are organized as an escalating sequence of five policies, from no targeting through selection-absent targeting to selection-driven targeting, presented as successive rows rather than regression columns.
The empirical welfare objective is explicitly written as inverse-propensity weighted by the known randomization probabilities, with the weighting formula given directly in the specification equation.
Sample composition by arm is reported once in the experiment description and cross-referenced in a table note rather than repeated as an N row in every results table.

Because reusing the same data to learn and evaluate the policy biases the in-sample welfare estimate upward, the paper builds a synthetic test sample from cross-fitted residual resampling and derives confidence intervals from that test sample instead of standard regression standard errors.

Confidence intervals for maximal welfare gains are constructed as one-sided intervals under a standard-normal approximation, motivated by guarding against the upward bias from optimizing and evaluating on the same data.

No discussion of clustering standard errors appears anywhere in the text; inference relies entirely on the resampling test-sample procedure and IV asymptotics, with clustering neither used nor discussed as an alternative.
Standard errors for the LATE-style mechanism estimates rely on the randomization of the arm assignment conditional on covariates rather than any explicit clustering or bootstrap procedure.
A combined summary-statistics and balance table reports mean differences with standard errors across the three randomized arms as the design's balance check.
A specification test targeting the testable inequality implications of the exclusion-type assumption is applied to the experimental data as a diagnostic for the mechanism analysis.

An empirical Monte Carlo study calibrated to resemble the experimental data is used to check the bias and coverage properties of the proposed inference procedure before it is applied to the real results.
A separate comparison sample of eligible non-participants from the same regions is described and used to characterize how the experimental sample differs from the broader population on observables.
The proposed cross-fitted resampling inference procedure is benchmarked in one table against a naive in-sample approach and a sample-splitting approach on bias, standard error, and coverage.

Because exact optimization of the full-depth policy tree is computationally infeasible, a two-step grafting heuristic is documented and justified by appeal to standard practice in the tree-classifier literature.
The welfare ranking is checked by comparing the optimized policy against several fixed, non-optimized benchmark policies rather than only against a single alternative specification.

Covariate distributions are broken out by the optimally assigned group to show which household characteristics are associated with each arm, framed as an input to interpreting the mechanism rather than a formal heterogeneity table.

The take-up rate achieved under the self-selection arm is discussed relative to take-up rates reported for critical-peak-pricing programs in prior studies, attributed partly to the rebate design never penalizing participants financially.

Welfare gains across all five compared policies are expressed on one common per-household-per-season monetary scale that nets consumption benefits against implementation costs, allowing direct cross-policy comparison.

The non-targeted benchmark policies are described as producing welfare gains that are not, or only marginally, statistically distinguishable from zero, used to motivate the targeting policies as the more informative comparison.

Authors note that because their experiment only includes households who agreed to participate, findings pertain to this self-selected experimental population, a limitation described as common in the residential electricity-demand literature.

Authors are explicit that the exclusion-type assumption used for the mechanism analysis is not required for the paper's headline welfare-assignment results, isolating which conclusions rest on the stronger assumption.

The summary-statistics and balance table reports means with standard deviations in brackets and mean differences with standard errors in parentheses, a bracket-and-parenthesis convention repeated in later tables.
The mechanism section presents the taker and non-taker LATE point estimates with confidence intervals in a figure rather than a results table.
Welfare-comparison tables report point estimates, standard errors, and exact p-values for pairwise comparisons instead of using significance-star notation.

The theoretical section includes a schematic figure partitioning a two-dimensional characteristic space into labeled regions to illustrate how the optimal-assignment characterization sorts individuals.
The introduction previews the composition of the optimal assignment across arms and the direction of the main welfare comparison before the formal model and empirical sections are presented.

A dedicated paragraph situates the paper against three literatures, targeting methods in economics, hybrid-choice designs in medical statistics, and the statistical treatment-choice literature, stating what is new relative to each.
The full theoretical framework and identification argument are presented before the field experiment and data are introduced, so the estimand is defined independently of the specific application.
The mechanism analysis using the LATE framework is placed in its own section after the main welfare-assignment results rather than being interleaved with the main results.
The Monte Carlo validation of the inference procedure is kept as the final subsection of the main results section rather than deferred to an appendix.

A replication package identifier is cited in the end matter, and the journal states it verified the package's ability to reproduce the paper's results using a simplified version of the code because of the algorithms' computational demands.
observations.quote: the reproducibility checks were run on a simplified version of the code

observations.statement: Specific estimation software components, including a policy-tree search algorithm and causal or random-forest routines, are named in the estimation-details subsection without a separate software-availability statement.
The paper states its trial registration with the AEA RCT Registry, without further discussion of a pre-analysis plan or its deviations in the main text.

The paper frames its estimated LATEs and optimal assignment as pertaining to the population of households who opted into the experiment, and separately compares this sample to eligible non-participants on observables.

The rebate program's cost and price parameters are calibrated to the Japanese electricity market during the specific experimental period, which is relevant to how the welfare calculation would transfer elsewhere.

Analysis combines high-frequency household electricity-usage records with a pre-experiment survey collecting household demographic and attitudinal variables, gathered specifically for this study rather than drawn from an existing public dataset.

The end-matter statement explains that some underlying data could not be publicly released due to restricted access rights, and describes that the journal separately obtained temporary access to check reproducibility.

concordance.paper_says: Optimal policy is estimated by empirical welfare maximization over depth-6 decision trees, computed via a two-step heuristic that grafts a depth-3 child tree onto each branch of a depth-3 parent tree.
concordance.card_shows: Both specifications call two_step_ewm_tree(..., depth = c(3,3)) from the policytree package, matching the two-step depth-3/depth-3 grafting heuristic, but the card's own structured estimator field is left null.

concordance.paper_says: The assignment rule is a nonparametric partition of the covariate space with no regression fixed effects involved.
concordance.card_shows: fixed_effects is null for both specifications, with no fixed-effect term appearing in the traced code.

concordance.paper_says: Confidence intervals for the welfare estimates come from a bespoke cross-fitted residual-resampling test-sample procedure with a one-sided normal approximation, not a conventional named standard-error type.
concordance.card_shows: se.type is null for both specifications; the resampling and cross-fitting script that produces the reported intervals was not traced into a specification-level standard-error record.

concordance.paper_says: No clustering of standard errors is discussed anywhere in the text.
concordance.card_shows: se.cluster_level is null for both specifications, consistent with no clustering being coded.

concordance.paper_says: The selection-absent targeting policy is restricted to choose only between the compulsory treated and untreated arms, while the selection-driven targeting policy chooses among all three arms including self-selection.
concordance.card_shows: The two traced specification calls use differently named input data objects, dta_sat for the first policy and dta for the second, consistent with a narrower assignable-arm set for the first policy; the structured sample field is null in both.

concordance.paper_says: Five policies are compared, with the fully untreated policy used as the reference welfare level against which the other four policies' gains are measured.
concordance.card_shows: comparison_group is null in the design record and in both specification records.

concordance.paper_says: Covariates selected via lasso and causal-forest importance rankings, pre-period consumption ratios and survey variables, are used as the tree-splitting covariates.
concordance.card_shows: controls_summary is null for both specifications; the traced call shows only X = select(dta, any_of(covariates)) without enumerating which variables the covariates object contains.

concordance.paper_says: The empirical welfare objective inversely weights each observation by its known randomization propensity score, with the weighting written explicitly into the estimating equation.
concordance.card_shows: weights is null for both specifications; the traced call at this line does not show the propensity weighting term.

concordance.paper_says: An instrument-validity specification test targeting the exclusion-type assumption is reported as a diagnostic for the mechanism analysis.
concordance.card_shows: The diagnostics array in the card is empty.

concordance.paper_says: An empirical Monte Carlo study compares the proposed inference procedure against a naive in-sample approach and a sample-splitting approach on bias, standard error, and coverage.
concordance.card_shows: The robustness array in the card is empty, and no evidence entries reference the Monte Carlo comparison script.

concordance.paper_says: The paper presents five main numbered tables and two main figures covering balance, welfare comparisons, covariate distributions, Monte Carlo validation, and the mechanism results.
concordance.card_shows: outputs.tables and outputs.figures are both empty arrays, and both specifications have empty output_ids, so no table or figure is linked to either traced specification.

concordance.paper_says: Data combine 30-minute household electricity-usage records and a pre-experiment household survey, collected in collaboration with a government ministry specifically for this study.
concordance.card_shows: The top-level data array in the card is empty; no data source entry was recorded from the traced code files.

gaps: No discussion of multiple-testing adjustment despite pairwise comparisons across five policies presented in two tables.
No explicit discussion of standard-error clustering at any level; inference relies solely on the resampling test-sample procedure and IV asymptotics.
No separate appendix or online supplementary section is present in this extracted text, although an online appendix is referenced as having been checked by the journal.
No explicit IRB or human-subjects ethics statement in the main text beyond the trial registry number.
No joint balance test or omnibus statistic reported for the three-arm randomization; only pairwise variable-by-variable differences appear in Table I.

reading.note: Read the full extracted text page by page, title through references and the end-matter replication statement. No appendix section is present in this extracted document; an online appendix is referenced as reviewed by the journal but is not part of this PDF extraction.
